subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
passage: On his third Saturday in Kolkata, Tanvir let the tram carry him past his stop just to see where it ended. He had already learned to say "khub bhalo" to the paan-shop owner and tried mishti doi from a clay pot, wincing at the sweetness and then asking for another. His colleague Damini took him to see the festival lights and explained why everyone dressed the way they did, and he asked so many questions that she laughed. He started leaving work later, like his team. But every Sunday he still called his mother in Hyderabad, and he cooked his own biryani for the flatmates, who lined up for seconds. "I'm collecting, not swapping," he told Damini.

qa.q: What did Tanvir cook for his flatmates?
qa.a: He cooked his own biryani for the flatmates.

qa.q: Why does Tanvir tell Damini "I'm collecting, not swapping"?
qa.a: Tanvir wants to add new customs and tastes without giving up his own. He is curious but feels no need to drop where he comes from.

qa.q: How can Tanvir decide what to adopt and what to keep?
qa.a: Adopt what helps, like the local greeting and the team's working hours, and stay rooted in what matters to him, like the Sunday calls and his own cooking.

qa.q: How does Damini seem to see Tanvir's many questions?
qa.a: She laughed, so she seems amused and welcoming, and she enjoyed explaining her city.

grounding: Exploring new customs, foods and work habits with interest while staying rooted in one's own culture, without copying blindly.

subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
passage:
Dear Parveen,

Four months in Osaka! I promised to tell you everything, so here goes.

Everyone takes off their shoes at the door, even at some offices. I love it now. Our flat will be a no-shoes flat when I'm back, warn Ammi. 😄

At work, meetings are so quiet. People don't interrupt. At first I thought nobody liked my ideas. Now I've learned to send my points in writing before the meeting, and they actually get discussed. I'm keeping that habit forever.

Food: I've eaten raw fish, fermented beans and something I still can't name. Some I loved. The beans, never again.

But I haven't changed everything. I still do my namaz in the small room at the station, and on Fridays I bring biryani for my team. Last week my manager asked for the recipe.

I'm learning a lot. I'm also still very much your cousin Leela.

qa.q: What does Leela bring for the team on Fridays?
What was Leela feeling at the first quiet meetings in Osaka?
qa.a: Leela felt unsure and a little discouraged, thinking nobody liked the ideas.

qa.q: Which new habit is Leela keeping, and why is it a good choice?
qa.a: Sending points in writing before meetings, because it adapts to how the office works and gets Leela's ideas discussed.

qa.q: How might Leela's manager see the Friday biryani?
qa.a: The manager seems curious and pleased, enough to ask for the recipe.

grounding: The letter shows someone exploring new customs, food and ways of working with curiosity, adapting where it helps and staying rooted in their own faith and food.

subtopic: Moving abroad or to a new city
passage:
"Ira, you asked what Chennai's been like. I'm Bhupen, I came from Jorhat for this job, and honestly, it's been a year of learning.

The first week I couldn't handle the heat or the filter coffee, too strong. Now I can't start my day without it. My colleague's mother taught me to make rasam; I make it on Sundays, but I still add a little bamboo shoot, which horrifies her.

The work culture was different too. Everyone calls the boss 'sir' even when he's younger. I tried it for a month and it felt strange, so I compromised: polite, but I use his name when we're alone, and he doesn't mind.

What I haven't changed: I still speak Assamese on my calls home, and during Bihu I cooked for twelve Tamil colleagues. They danced terribly. I loved it.

So I'm changing, Ira. Just not into someone else."

qa.q: What does Bhupen add to rasam?
How does Bhupen feel about the changes of the past year, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Bhupen feels curious and happy about them, enjoying filter coffee and rasam now and loving the Bihu meal with colleagues.

qa.q: What balance did Bhupen find, and why does it work?
qa.a: Adapting to the coffee, food and politeness at work, while keeping the Assamese language and Bihu, which lets Bhupen learn without betraying home.

qa.q: How might Bhupen's Tamil colleagues see the Bihu meal?
qa.a: They likely enjoyed it and felt welcomed into Bhupen's culture, even if they danced badly.

grounding: The spoken account shows someone exploring a new city's food and customs with curiosity, adapting where helpful and staying rooted in their own language and festivals.
